title: Joshua 9:1–15
context: News of Jericho and Ai moves the kings of Canaan to unite against Israel, but the people of Gibeon take another path. Disguised as envoys from a distant land, with worn sacks, patched sandals, and moldy bread, they ask for a covenant. The Israelite leaders examine the provisions but do not ask counsel from the LORD, and Joshua and the princes make peace and swear an oath to let them live. The scene recalls Deuteronomy’s distinction between distant cities and the peoples of the land (Deuteronomy 7:2; 20:10–18).

verses.text: When all the kings who were beyond the Jordan, in the hill country, and in the lowland, and on all the shore of the great sea in front of Lebanon, the Hittite, the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite, heard of it
verses.arminianNotes: A coalition forms west of the Jordan among the peoples Deuteronomy names (Deuteronomy 7:1). Arminian readers see the kings responding to the same reports of God’s acts that moved Rahab to faith (2:9–11), but choosing resistance instead.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the list of six peoples marks these nations as the ones under judgment in the land. Shared ground: the verse sets up a contrast between united resistance and the different response of Gibeon that follows.

verses.text: they gathered themselves together to fight with Joshua and with Israel, with one accord.
verses.arminianNotes: The kings gather with one accord to fight Joshua and Israel. Arminian readers observe that hearing of God’s works does not compel a single response; the nations hear the same news and choose opposition rather than seeking peace.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the alliance as the nations hardening themselves against Israel, a theme stated outright in 11:20. Both traditions read the united front as human hostility to God’s purpose for His people in the land.

verses.text: But when the inhabitants of Gibeon heard what Joshua had done to Jericho and to Ai,
verses.arminianNotes: Gibeon hears the same report as the kings but responds differently. Arminian readers find here a case where fear of God’s acts leads a people to seek terms with Israel, even if the means they choose is deceptive.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Gibeon, though one of the peoples of the land, ends up spared and later serving at the altar. Shared ground: the narrative contrasts Gibeon’s response with the coalition’s, without approving the method used.

verses.text: they also resorted to a ruse, and went and made as if they had been ambassadors, and took old sacks on their donkeys, and old, torn-up and bound up wineskins,
verses.arminianNotes: The Gibeonites resort to a ruse, posing as envoys with worn sacks and wineskins. Arminian readers do not excuse the deception, yet note the narrative’s interest in a people trying to escape judgment by attaching themselves to Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise treat the trick as deception that Joshua will rebuke (9:22). Both traditions agree that the text describes the ruse without commending it, and that God’s purposes are not dependent on human honesty to advance.

verses.text: and old and patched sandals on their feet, and wore old garments. All the bread of their food supply was dry and moldy.
verses.arminianNotes: The patched sandals, old garments, and moldy bread are props meant to suggest a long journey. Arminian readers see careful staging aimed at Israel’s leaders, who will rely on what they can see rather than on inquiry of God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the detail as narrative preparation for 9:14, where sight-based testing replaces prayer. Shared ground: the props are crafted to fit the law’s provision for distant cities (Deuteronomy 20:15), which the envoys appear to know.

verses.text: They went to Joshua at the camp at Gilgal, and said to him and to the men of Israel, “We have come from a far country. Now therefore make a covenant with us.”
verses.arminianNotes: At Gilgal the envoys claim a far country and ask for a covenant. Arminian readers note that the request is shaped to fit what the law allows, since Israel could make peace with distant cities but not with the peoples of the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the request as testing whether Israel will keep God’s word about covenants in Canaan (Deuteronomy 7:2). Both traditions read the scene as a challenge to discernment: the claim may be false, and the leaders must test it.

verses.text: The men of Israel said to the Hivites, “What if you live among us? How could we make a covenant with you?”
verses.arminianNotes: The men of Israel voice the right concern: if these Hivites live nearby, no covenant is allowed. Arminian readers credit Israel with suspicion at first, which makes the later failure to ask the LORD more pointed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the narrator names them Hivites, one of the peoples of the land, so readers know the truth before Israel does. Shared ground: Israel knows the law’s boundary, and the question is whether it will apply it faithfully.

verses.text: They said to Joshua, “We are your servants.” Joshua said to them, “Who are you? Where do you come from?”
verses.arminianNotes: The envoys answer evasively, calling themselves servants instead of saying who they are. Arminian readers note Joshua’s sensible questions and the way the visitors avoid giving their names or city to the leader of Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the language of servitude anticipating the role the Gibeonites will actually receive (9:21–27). Both traditions note that the narrative lets the evasion show without comment, inviting readers to see what Joshua misses.

verses.text: They said to him, “Your servants have come from a very far country because of the name of the LORD your God; for we have heard of his fame, all that he did in Egypt,
verses.arminianNotes: The envoys say they came because of the name of the LORD and His deeds in Egypt. Arminian readers note the similarity to Rahab’s confession (2:10) and see a genuine, if fearful, recognition of Israel’s God mixed with deceit.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also hear a real acknowledgment of the LORD’s fame, though offered as part of a deception. Shared ground: news of God’s acts reaches the nations, and Gibeon’s words, whatever their motive, honor His name.

verses.text: and all that he did to the two kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan, to Sihon king of Heshbon and to Og king of Bashan, who was at Ashtaroth.
verses.arminianNotes: The envoys mention Sihon and Og east of the Jordan but leave out Jericho and Ai. Arminian readers see this as calculated: a truly distant people would only have heard of older victories, so the omission supports the cover story.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same careful selection and see the narrative inviting readers to admire the craft while recognizing the lie. Both traditions read the omission of recent victories as part of the ruse rather than as a gap in knowledge.

verses.text: Our elders and all the inhabitants of our country spoke to us, saying, ‘Take supplies in your hand for the journey, and go to meet them. Tell them, “We are your servants. Now make a covenant with us.” ’
verses.arminianNotes: The envoys quote their elders’ instructions to seek a covenant and call themselves Israel’s servants. Arminian readers see a community decision behind the embassy, a corporate choice to seek terms rather than to fight.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the elders’ plan, though deceptive, is the means through which Gibeon is spared. Shared ground: the request for a covenant is presented as a deliberate act of the whole community, not a few individuals.

verses.text: This our bread we took hot for our supplies out of our houses on the day we went out to go to you; but now, behold, it is dry, and has become moldy.
verses.arminianNotes: The bread, hot when packed and now dry and moldy, is offered as evidence. Arminian readers see how persuasive physical proof can be, and how it can crowd out the further step of asking God for guidance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the evidence is false but appears convincing, a reminder that outward appearances can mislead even careful leaders. Both traditions use the scene to stress the limits of human judgment without seeking God.

verses.text: These wineskins, which we filled, were new; and behold, they are torn. These our garments and our sandals have become old because of the very long journey.”
verses.arminianNotes: The torn wineskins and worn garments complete the story of a long journey. Arminian readers note the layering of details, each one designed to answer the suspicion Israel raised in 9:7 about whether they lived nearby.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the accumulation of props as building toward the narrator’s verdict in the next verse. Shared ground: the envoys’ case is crafted to persuade, and the narrative wants readers to feel how plausible it seemed.

verses.text: The men sampled their provisions, and didn’t ask counsel from the LORD’s mouth.
verses.arminianNotes: The men sampled the provisions but did not ask counsel from the LORD. Arminian readers see this as the key failure: Israel had the means to inquire of God and neglected it, relying instead on its own inspection.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that the failure lies in not seeking the LORD, and note that God’s providence still works through Israel’s mistake. Shared ground: both traditions read this verse as the narrator’s judgment that prayerless decision-making led Israel astray.

verses.text: Joshua made peace with them, and made a covenant with them, to let them live. The princes of the congregation swore to them.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua makes peace and a covenant to let them live, and the princes swear an oath. Arminian readers note that the oath is a real commitment made by responsible leaders, whose decision now binds Israel even though it was obtained by deceit.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the oath, sworn by the LORD (9:18), carries weight because of the name invoked. Both traditions agree that the covenant was made in error, yet becomes binding and shapes how Israel must act from here on.
